source: (1) GitClear, 'AI Copilot Code Quality: Evaluating 2024's Increased Defect Rate with Data' ('211m lines of analyzed code + projections for 2025'), William Harding, Lead Researcher & CEO, Alloy.dev Research, 'Published January, 2025', version label 'GitClear AI Code Quality Research v2025.2.4 Beta' (from the cover image on the landing page). Opened landing page with abstract and chart: https://www.gitclear.com/ai_assistant_code_quality_2025_research . Full PDF is behind an email form and was NOT opened. (2) Follow-up: GitClear, 'The Maintainability Gap: AI Code Quality in 2026' (same content also published as 'Write-Only Mode: AI Code Quality in 2026'). Opened landing pages with abstract: https://www.gitclear.com/the_ai_code_quality_maintainability_gap and https://www.gitclear.com/write_only_mode_ai_research . Full PDF gated, not opened; no author or exact publication date shown on the pages opened.
data_type: Telemetry: commit and code-change line analysis (repository data), observational trend over time. No direct attribution of each line to AI.
sample_and_method: 2025: '211 million changed lines of code, authored between January 2020 and December 2024, are assessed on quantifiable "code quality" metrics' from 'repos owned by Google, Microsoft, Meta, and enterprise C-Corps' (landing page). LeadDev adds 'anonymized private repositories and 25 of the largest open-source projects' [uncertain] (secondary). Lines are classified by operation (added, deleted, updated, moved, copy/pasted, find/replace). The comparison is by calendar year, with 2023 to 2024 shaded 'AI Influenced' on the chart, not AI vs non-AI lines; the landing page asks whether there are 'measurable differences in code quality metrics between AI-assisted blocks and non-AI-assisted code' but the visible data is year-on-year. 2026: '623 million analyzed changes from 2023-2026', tracking 'eight quality signals' in the subtitle and 'seven distinct code-quality signals' in the abstract; 2026 values are 'year-to-date' (first half of 2026). Recruitment of repos and per-repo counts not given on the pages opened.
vendor_interest: Yes. GitClear sells developer analytics, code review and code-quality measurement tools (Diff Delta, PR review, AI code-quality charts), and the 2026 page promotes 'Live-updating AI code-quality graphs' and 'measure structure, not (just) volume'. It does not sell an AI coding assistant. The reports are lead-generation assets gated behind a business email form.
headline_figures: 2025 landing page abstract: 'The research finds that the percentage of changed code lines (associated with refactoring) sunk from 25% of changed lines in 2021, to less than 10% in 2024, while lines classified as "copy/pasted" (cloned) rose from 8.3% to 12.3% in the same period.' / Page title: '2025 Data Suggests 4x Growth in Code Clones'; strapline: 'Emerging trends: 4x more code cloning, "copy/paste" exceeds "moved" code for first time in history.' / 'We observe a spike in the prevalence of duplicate code blocks, along with increases in short-term churn code, and the continued decline of moved lines (code reuse).' Chart 'Percent of Commits Containing a Cloned Code Block' (read from the image, approximate): about 0.7% (2020), 0.5% (2021), 0.45% (2022), 1.8% (2023), 6.7% (2024). 2026 abstract on the 2025 report: 'documented that 2024 was the first year on record where within-commit copy/paste exceeded "moved" (refactored) code, and that commits containing a duplicated block rose roughly 10x over two years.' 2026 Maintainability Gap: 'cross-file function calls (indicative of reuse) are down 35%. Refactoring line moves are down 70%, and long-term legacy maintenance is down 74% vs 2022 levels.' / 'within-commit copy/paste (+41%), code block duplication (+81%), error-masking constructs (+47%), and two-week code churn (+15%).' / 'block duplication climbed from 40.3 in 2023 to 73.0 year-to-date in 2026 — an 81% increase over 2023' (per million changed lines). / 'the percentage of moved code dropped to 13% of changed lines in 2023, before freefalling to 3.8% year-to-date in 2026. Over the same window, copy/paste climbed from 9.4% (in 2022) to 15.7% in the first half of 2026.' / 'Function connectivity... has fallen 35% since 2023, from 343 method calls per thousand changed lines to 223 year-to-date.' / 'Long-term update percent... has fallen 74%, from 1.7% in 2023 to 0.46% year-to-date in 2026.' Secondary only [uncertain]: LeadDev reports an '8-fold increase in the frequency of code blocks with five or more lines that duplicate adjacent code' in 2024 and '46% of code changes were new lines'; a secondary churn figure of 3.3% (2021) to 5.7% (2024) was seen in search results but not in any GitClear page opened.
metric_layer: Quality and maintainability of code changes (activity/output layer, structural quality): duplication, copy/paste, moved (refactored) lines, churn, cross-file calls, legacy updates, error-masking. No usage, delivery or financial outcome measures. The 2026 page mentions a separate January 2026 GitClear study on velocity (activity layer).
respondent_role_split: Not applicable: telemetry, no respondents. The 2026 page says the debt 'concentrates among developers who haven't recognized the failure modes', and its January 2026 study split heavy AI users from non-users ('heavy AI users out-produce non-users by 4–10x, but most of that gap pre-dated AI — compared to their past selves, heavy AI users enjoyed a more modest 25% velocity gain'). There is no IC/manager/executive split.
workload_signal: Indirect only. Duplication is framed as a future workload cost: 'when a developer changes one copy of a five-line block, they inherit the obligation to find and evaluate every sibling' (2026). Two-week churn up 15% (2026) suggests rework. Legacy maintenance down 74% implies deferred work. No hours, time correcting AI, pressure or burnout measured on the pages opened.
definition_of_value_offered: Yes, in maintainability terms. 2025 abstract: 'if you ask a Senior Developer "what would unlock your team's full potential?" their answer won't be "more code lines added." To retain high project velocity over years, research suggests that a DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself), modular approach to building is essential.' It asks how 'today's profusion of LLM-authored code is influencing the maintainability of tomorrow's systems.' 2026: the cost that matters is 'how expensive a codebase is to own in year three'; recommendations: '(1) budget for refactoring and legacy maintenance, (2) put a tripwire on duplicate blocks, (3) review for error-masking explicitly, (4) direct coaching where judgment is thinnest, (5) measure structure, not (just) volume.' It argues lines added or commit count is the wrong measure of payoff but gives no financial method.
removal_counterfactual: None. The comparison is pre-AI years (2020 to 2022) vs AI-influenced years (2023 onward), not tool removal. The 2026 page cites 2022 as 'the final year of Pre-AI', when a 'Coding on Copilot' report showed 'a 2x preference for refactor over redundant', as a historical baseline.
key_quotes: 1. 'The throughput is real, but so is the debt it accrues' (GitClear, The Maintainability Gap, 2026). 2. 'The biggest risk isn't that AI writes code your team can't maintain. It's that it writes that code faster than ever, and the bill arrives when you can least afford it.' (GitClear, The Maintainability Gap, 2026).
caveats: Correlation over time, not causation: the data shows trends during the years AI assistants spread, and the visible material does not attribute each duplicated block to AI. Industry-wide changes in the repo mix over time could also affect results. Duplication multiples conflict across GitClear's own write-ups and press coverage: '4x' (2025 landing page; matches the 2023 to 2024 chart rise), 'roughly 10x over two years' (2026 abstract; matches 2022 to 2024), and '8-fold' (LeadDev, secondary). Use the precise metric and years when citing. The 2026 page says refactoring moves are 'down 70%', but its own figures (21% in 2022 to 3.8% in 2026) imply about an 82% fall, and the 13% (2023) to 3.8% fall is about 71%, so the base year for the 70% is unclear. It also says 'eight' signals in one place and 'seven' in another. 2026 values are partial-year. The 2025 refactoring figure is phrased as moved lines 'associated with refactoring', a proxy. Vendor-produced, not peer reviewed, and the PDFs are gated.
access: Partly opened. Opened: 2025 landing page (abstract, cover image, cloned-block chart) and 2026 Maintainability Gap / Write-Only Mode landing pages (extended abstract). Not opened: either full PDF (gated behind business-email form; not submitted). Not verified against primary: the 8x duplication figure, the 46% new-lines figure, the dataset composition ('25 of the largest open-source projects'), and any churn percentages for 2021 to 2024 [uncertain]. Chart values are read from an image and are approximate.
